title: Technology and worship
hookLine: prayer apps, online Qur'an, and the need for real presence

lines: AN OLD REPORT FOR A NEW MOMENT.
cards: The app chimes. 'Asr, it says, and a little compass on the screen swings around to point toward Mecca. The mat goes down, the phone beside it, face up, and the prayer begins.
Second rak'ah, forehead on the floor, and the screen lights up: a name, half a message. The prayer carries on. The mind doesn't, quite.
What does a phone in the pocket do to a prayer? An old report in al-Bukhari fits.

teach.b: The report is told by 'Aisha. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once prayed in a garment with markings on it, a patterned cloth, and during the prayer his eye caught the pattern.
When he finished he said, in paraphrase: take this to Abu Jahm and bring me his plain one, because this one just distracted me in my prayer.
Right beside it, al-Bukhari keeps a second report, about a curtain with pictures hanging in 'Aisha's house.

The Prophet asked for it to be taken down, because its pictures kept coming to him while he prayed. He didn't give up clothes, or curtains. He swapped the one thing that kept pulling at his attention for something plain.

teach.h: THE TOOL STAYS. THE DISTRACTION GOES.
teach.b: The tool stayed. The distraction went. The Qur'an has a word for what was being protected.
The chapter called The Believers opens, in Pickthall's translation: "Successful indeed are the believers / Who are humble in their prayers."

teach.h: KHUSHU': THE WHOLE PERSON TURNED ONE WAY.
teach.b: Muslim teachers call that humility in prayer khushu': stillness, lowered eyes, the whole person turned one way.

And in the conversation with the angel Gabriel, the Prophet describes ihsan, doing a thing beautifully, in paraphrase: to worship Allah as though you see Him, and though you don't see Him, He sees you. That is presence.
So the question about technology is an old one. An app that tells you when Maghrib comes is a timetable. A screen that shows the Qur'an is a page.
Both can serve the prayer. 'Aisha's report asks something simpler and harder: what keeps coming to you while you pray, and can you hand it to Abu Jahm?

how: Muslims today may use apps or printed timetables for prayer times and the direction of the qibla, and some put the phone on silent or in another room before they pray.

o: apps and screens that can serve a prayer, but can't supply presence
prayer done online, so that a mosque is no longer needed
a ruling that phones and apps are forbidden near prayer

games.q: presence in prayer — tap the pairs.
p: sent to Abu Jahm for a plain one
taken down; its pictures kept coming
worship as though you see Him

s: the Prophet threw the distracting garment away
he sent it to Abu Jahm and asked for Abu Jahm's plain one instead.
the Qur'an links success to being humble in prayer
"successful indeed are the believers / who are humble in their prayers" (23:1–2, Pickthall).
the old reports say nothing about distraction in prayer
al-Bukhari keeps two side by side: a patterned garment and a curtain with pictures.

games.q: you're praying in a new patterned garment, and the pattern keeps catching your eye. the prayer ends. what do you do?
o: stop wearing anything that could ever distract.
give it away and ask for a plain one.
keep it, and just try harder not to look.
games.why: the Prophet sent it to Abu Jahm and asked for his plain garment, saying it had distracted him in prayer. the cloth went; the clothes stayed.

practice: Set the phone in another room, or face down out of reach, and notice any pull toward it, an itch to check; don't fight it, just notice it, the way the Prophet noticed the pattern on the cloth.
Then let your attention come back to one thing: your breath, the room around you, or, if you pray, al-Fatiha said slowly in your head. When the pull comes again, notice it, and come back again.

wordCard.voice: Technology and worship. Apps, screens and timetables that can serve a prayer, and the presence that no tool can supply. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: humble stillness and full attention in prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: real presence. The tool stays; the distraction goes. Back tomorrow, same hill.
